issues.issue: The sentence "a Beneficiary may request written election of any such other plans in lieu of a lump sum" is garbled and leaves unclear whether the Company must honour such a request or merely receive it. The grant of alternative settlement options is expressed only as a possibility ("If the Company makes other plans of payment available").

The Schedule lists a Risk Classification of "Percentage Substandard 150.0%" but states "Additional Ratings Not Applicable", while Section 9's Monthly Deduction component (d) charges for "any applicable Additional Ratings shown in Section 1". How the 150% substandard rating is charged is left unreconciled.

The notice requires "the Net Policy Value, less Policy Debt" to cover deductions, but Section 3 already defines Net Policy Value as the Policy Value less Policy Debt, so the phrase double-subtracts the debt. That mechanical error changes the lapse threshold it purports to describe.

The charge table has been reproduced with the descriptions detached from the charge names, so which text ($50.00, $3.50, 3.5%) belongs to which charge is not fixed on the face of the page. The Surrender Charge also appears under the heading "Monthly Deduction" though it is not a monthly deduction under Section 9.

Section 15 conditions withdrawals on the "Minimum Face Amount shown in Section 1", but this Table of Values contains only a "Minimum Total Face Amount" and a "Minimum Basic Face Amount" and no term of that name. The cross-reference cannot be matched to any entry here.

This footnote asserts an unqualified right to "change ... the amount of cost of insurance deducted", while Section 9 states that cost of insurance rates "will be based on our expectations of future mortality, persistency, investment earnings, expense experience, capital and reserve requirements, and tax assumptions" and must not discriminate unfairly. Whether the Section 1 footnote frees the insurer from the Section 9 constraints is a live question.

The Monthly Factor is stated as "4.0032737" where the parallel non-unisex paragraph states 1.0032737; a factor of 4 would quadruple the divisor used to compute the Net Amount at Risk. That is a mechanical error that changes the arithmetic the clause prescribes.

"Attained Age" is defined as "the Age plus the number of whole years that have elapsed since the Policy Date", but "Age" is itself defined as the person's age at the nearest birthday on the given date, so elapsed years are counted twice. Read literally the Insured reaches Attained Age 100 fourteen years before the Maturity Date.

On its literal terms this definition cannot be squared with the Section 3 definition of "Maturity Date" ("the date upon which the Insured reaches Attained Age 100") and the October 12, 2035 Maturity Date shown in Section 1. The two produce different Age-100 dates.

"Due proof of death" is defined by two specifics followed by the open catch-all "any other proof acceptable to us", leaving the reach of the catch-all and the insurer's discretion to reject proof undefined. Death Proceeds are payable only "on receipt ... of due proof", so the boundary matters.

"In force" is tied only to termination or lapse "in accordance with the Grace Period provision", but Section 12 lists two further automatic termination events (death of the Insured and surrender). The definition and the termination section do not cover the same ground.

The definition requires "a written form signed by you, satisfactory to us" but then adds "or such other medium electronic or otherwise that we may from time to time make available", so whether an electronic communication satisfies the signature requirement is left open. The syntax does not make clear what the alternative medium is an alternative to.

The "Issue Date" is defined only by its function ("the date from which the Suicide Exclusion and Incontestability provisions are applied") and not by any identifiable event, making the definition circular. Its content depends entirely on the Schedule entry it does not reference.

The stated Maturity Date of October 12, 2035 depends on "Attained Age 100", but the Section 3 definition of Attained Age (Age plus whole years elapsed since the Policy Date) would place Attained Age 100 much earlier. The two cannot both be right.

The Section 1 premium notice speaks of "the Net Policy Value, less Policy Debt", which subtracts Policy Debt a second time from a figure this definition already nets. The lapse test therefore reads differently in Section 1 than in Section 11.

The opening formula — Net Premium credited "less an amount not to exceed one month of Monthly Deductions" — gives no rule for fixing the amount actually deducted within that ceiling. The initial Policy Value is therefore not determinable from the definition itself.

The Living Benefit Rider defines "We (Our, Us)" as "Phoenix Life Insurance Company, or its subsidiaries", whereas this definition limits the pronouns to the Company alone. The two definitions of the same pronouns do not match.

"We reserve the right to make any reasonable adjustments to the terms or conditions of this policy ... to the extent we deem it necessary" combines an objective standard ("reasonable") with a wholly subjective trigger ("we deem"), and no limit on what terms may be adjusted. The scope of that unilateral power is not fixed by the words.

This clause lets the Company adjust policy terms unilaterally "notwithstanding any other provisions of the policy to the contrary", while Section 22 provides that any change in the provisions of the policy must be in writing signed by an executive officer and countersigned. The two amendment mechanisms sit uneasily together.

The reserved "right to refuse any premium payments that would cause the policy to fail the test you elected" is contradicted by the closing sentence of the Guideline Premium Limit paragraph: "In no event, however, will we refuse to accept any premium necessary to prevent the policy from terminating."

The closing sentence ("In no event, however, will we refuse to accept any premium necessary to prevent the policy from terminating") cannot be squared with Section 10's directive that "we will not process such payment" where receipt would disqualify the policy as life insurance, or with Section 4's reserved right to refuse such premiums.

A face-amount reduction here triggers a pro-rata Surrender Charge, whereas the Section 6 reduction on a change of Death Benefit Option is made "with no change to the surrender charge schedule of the policy". Which rule governs a reduction achieved through an option change is not stated.

The rule that "if the Insured dies on or after the date we receive a request from you to surrender the policy, no Death Proceeds will be paid" is hard to reconcile with Section 12, under which the policy terminates only on "the date the policy is surrendered", and with the Grace Period rule preserving proceeds on death. The date coverage ends is stated differently in the two sections.

This paragraph reduces Death Proceeds by "any outstanding Policy Charges due", while Section 11 says that on death in default "we will deduct from the proceeds all Monthly Deductions due and unpaid". Policy Charges is a broader category than Monthly Deductions.

The statement that a withdrawal reduces the Death Benefit by reducing "the Policy Value if Option B is in effect" sits against Section 15, which spells out that under Option B the withdrawal comes out of Policy Value and "the Total Face Amount does not change". The two descriptions of the same event are stated at different levels and could be read to differ.

The insurer may cut back the Minimum Death Benefit where the Net Amount at Risk "exceeds our guidelines and limitations that may be in effect", a standard that is nowhere defined or disclosed in the policy. The insured cannot tell from the contract when the reduction right arises.

Section 8 provides that on the Age 100 Anniversary an Option B policy changes to Option A, "which means the Total Face Amount will not be increased by the Policy Value" — the opposite of the rule stated here for a B-to-A change. The exception and the general rule point in different directions.

This says a reduction in Total Face Amount occurs "with no change to the surrender charge schedule", while Section 5 requires a pro-rata Surrender Charge to be deducted on any reduction in Total Face Amount. The two treatments of the same event conflict.

The second sentence — "You are limited to one surrender charges for this policy" — is missing its object (evidently "change in Death Benefit Option per Policy Year") and is ungrammatical, so the limitation it imposes cannot be read off the words. As written it states no intelligible restriction.

The test compares "total premiums paid by you less partial withdrawals, since policy issue, less policy debt" against cumulative Monthly Guarantee Premiums, but the placement of "since policy issue" and the deduction of policy debt leave the computation open to more than one reading. Whether accrued loan interest reduces the test amount is not clear.

The clause says that on a change in face amount, rider or risk classification "we will modify the Monthly Guarantee Premium" without stating any basis, formula or limit for the modification. The revised figure that determines the no-lapse guarantee is left to the insurer's unstated method.

Section 6 provides that on a "Change from Option B to Option A: the Total Face Amount will be increased by the Policy Value", whereas this bullet says the same change at Age 100 means "the Total Face Amount will not be increased by the Policy Value". The two provisions state opposite consequences for the same conversion.

The post-100 Death Benefit is the greater of Total Face Amount or Policy Value, which omits the Section 6 Minimum Death Benefit (Policy Value times the applicable percentage) that the opening words of Section 8 say continues to apply "except as follows". Whether the Minimum Death Benefit survives after Age 100 is unsettled.

The flat statement that after the Age 100 Anniversary "we will not accept any further premium payments" cannot be squared with Section 4's promise that "in no event ... will we refuse to accept any premium necessary to prevent the policy from terminating", given that Section 8 keeps the default rules alive after Age 100.

Default here is cured under Section 11 by "payment of additional premiums or repayment of policy debt", but the immediately preceding paragraph of Section 8 bars any further premium payments after Age 100. The cure mechanism is partly unavailable in the very period this paragraph governs.

Component (d) charges for "any applicable Additional Ratings shown in Section 1", but Section 1 records "Additional Ratings Not Applicable" while classifying the Insured as 150% substandard. Where the substandard loading is charged is left unexplained.

The clause states that cost of insurance rates "are based on" an enumerated list of factors (sex, Age, Risk Classification, face amounts, Net Amount at Risk and duration), leaving open whether that list is exhaustive and whether rates may reflect factors not listed. "Based on" does not say whether the listed items are the only permissible inputs.

This list of rate factors, fixed "as of the Policy Date", stands against the Section 1 footnote asserting a right to "change ... the amount of cost of insurance deducted" and against the redetermination paragraph later in Section 9. Which controls a later rate increase is contestable.

"[S]uch rates will be based on our expectations of future mortality, persistency, investment earnings, expense experience, capital and reserve requirements, and tax assumptions" enumerates permitted factors without saying whether the list is exhaustive or whether every listed factor must actually change. "Based on our expectations" is also open to reading either as a substantive constraint or as a mere description.

This constraint on the rate basis is in tension with the Section 1 Table of Values footnote, which states flatly that "We have the right to change ... the amount of cost of insurance deducted under the policy" with no stated limitation. Whether the footnote qualifies the Section 9 limits is a genuine question.

"[A]ny adjustment for the Minimum Death Benefit" is not identified or quantified anywhere, and the Net Amount at Risk formula that follows already builds in the Minimum Death Benefit Percentage. The sentence's operative content is uncertain.

The redetermination power is limited only by a requirement that it be "on a basis that does not discriminate unfairly within any class of insureds", where neither "discriminate unfairly" nor "class of insureds" is defined. Whether the insurer may single out a subgroup within a rate class turns entirely on those words.

The unqualified permission to "re-determine Cost of Insurance rates" must be read with the preceding sentence limiting rates to the insurer's expectations of the enumerated factors and with the Section 1 footnote asserting an unrestricted right to change charges. The three passages give different accounts of the same power.

The formula subtracts (a) from the greater of (b) or (c), but (c) is itself defined as (a) multiplied by the Minimum Death Benefit Percentage, and limb (b) is set out in a garbled clause covering both Death Benefit Options at once. The arithmetic that produces the Net Amount at Risk is not unambiguously stated.

The interest-crediting sentence is broken mid-way, so the words tying the credited rate to the insurer's "anticipation of future investment earnings, mortality, persistency, expense and administrative costs, and taxes" have no grammatical subject; that standard then sits beside "We may, in our sole discretion, change the interest rate(s)." Whether crediting is constrained by the listed anticipations or purely discretionary is left open.

The rate table is internally garbled: the second band gives "50%" as an Additional Interest Rate (evidently 0.50%), and the columns are labelled so that a higher credited rate on unloaned Policy Value produces the larger bonus. The Additional Interest actually payable cannot be computed with confidence from the table as printed.

This exception is numbered "(i)", the same numeral as the preceding exception, so the two items in the list are not distinguished. The mislabelling obscures which exception a cross-reference to "(i)" picks up.

The refusal to process any premium that would disqualify the policy as a life insurance contract contradicts Section 4's promise that "in no event, however, will we refuse to accept any premium necessary to prevent the policy from terminating." A premium can fall within both descriptions.

The middle of the paragraph is broken ("Unless we agree oth === are subject to the Maximum Annual Premium sho ... Overloan Protection, no further premiums may be paid once Overlo: goes into effect"), so the qualification on the right to pay additional premiums and the Maximum Annual Premium limit cannot be read as written. The operative restriction is missing words.

The reserved right to "limit the number and amount of premium payments in any Policy Year" cuts against the same section's grant that "you may pay additional premiums at any time" and against Section 4's promise never to refuse a premium necessary to prevent termination. The extent of the insurer's veto over premiums is not settled.

The notice must be sent "at least 15 days and not more than 45 days prior to termination of coverage", which does not fit the 61-day grace period running from the date of default that the same section prescribes. When the notice obligation is triggered is left to inference.

The paragraph is missing its operative opening — the words granting the election and stating what the policy is "lapsed to" are gone — so the benefit's trigger and content cannot be read from the text. What survives is only the calculation basis for a benefit whose availability is unstated.

A reduced paid-up option is not among the outcomes recognised by Section 12, which says the policy "will terminate automatically" when the grace period expires, and the feature appears nowhere in the Table of Contents. The two provisions describe different fates for a lapsing policy.

The list of three automatic termination events is presented as exhaustive, yet Section 11 contemplates a Reduced Paid-Up Benefit on lapse and Section 14 keeps a policy in force through Overloan Protection. Whether the list truly accounts for every way coverage ends is open.

The paragraph begins mid-sentence ("request. A loan may not be taken after you have exercised Overloan Protecti"), so the sentence actually granting the right to borrow and stating its conditions is absent. The scope of the loan right must be supplied from outside the words.

The proviso that the Maximum Loan Value "will not be less than the Preferred Loan Amount plus accrued interest ... but in no event greater than the current Policy Value" can push the figure above limb (b), the current Surrender Value, contradicting the "lesser of (a) or (b)" rule in the same paragraph. Which cap governs is not stated.

The first sentence is truncated ("Loan interest will accrue on a daily basis from the date of"), leaving the accrual start date unstated. The rest of the paragraph presupposes a rule the text no longer contains.

"[A] change in the Interest Rate" is capitalised but undefined, and the sentence sits in the loan-interest paragraph, so it may mean the credited interest rate under Section 9 or the policy loan interest rate. Which rate triggers the anti-lapse protection is genuinely uncertain.

This anti-lapse promise has to be reconciled with Section 11, which makes default turn mechanically on whether Monthly Deductions exceed the Net Policy Value or Net Surrender Value regardless of cause. A rate change that produces such a shortfall engages both provisions.

The right to "repay the Policy Debt in whole or in part at any time prior to the death of the Insured and while the policy is in force" is contradicted by the Overloan Protection list, which provides that "[n]o additional loans or loan repayments will be allowed" once that feature is in effect. Both speak to the same in-force policy.

Condition 2 requires that "the Policy Debt is equal to 96% of the Policy Value" — an exact equality that would almost never obtain — where the following paragraph assumes a loan balance "in excess of 96%". The eligibility trigger as written is likely a mis-statement of an "at least" threshold.

Condition 2 (debt exactly equal to 96% of Policy Value) cannot be reconciled with the next paragraph, which contemplates exercise where "the loan balance is in excess of 96% of the Policy Value" and requires repayment of the excess. The two passages state different entry conditions.

This paragraph presupposes exercise while "the loan balance is in excess of 96% of the Policy Value", but the eligibility list immediately above permits exercise only when "the Policy Debt is equal to 96% of the Policy Value". The two cannot both be satisfied.

Reducing the Total Face Amount to 101% of Policy Value sits against Section 1's Minimum Total Face Amount of $100,000 and Section 5's requirement that reductions be subject to that minimum, with no statement of which prevails. It also triggers no pro-rata Surrender Charge although Section 5 requires one on any reduction.

The bar on all further premium payments conflicts with Section 4's undertaking that "in no event ... will we refuse to accept any premium necessary to prevent the policy from terminating". Nothing in either provision says which yields.

The prohibition on loan repayments contradicts the Loan Repayment paragraph of the same section, which allows repayment "at any time prior to the death of the Insured and while the policy is in force", and sits oddly with the requirement that excess loan balance be repaid on exercise. Loan interest meanwhile continues to accrue with no way to pay it.

The paragraph both imposes a one-time Overloan Transaction Charge (3.5% of Policy Value) and says "There is no additional charge for this benefit", and the sentence is cut off before its object. The reader cannot tell what is charged and what is free.

Condition (c) forbids a withdrawal reducing the Basic Face Amount below "the Minimum Face Amount shown in Section 1", but Section 1 contains no term of that name — only a Minimum Total Face Amount and a Minimum Basic Face Amount. The limit the condition imposes is not identified.

"Any benefits provided are not less than that required by law of the state where this policy was delivered" states an unquantified floor without identifying which law or which benefits it measures. Its operative effect on any particular calculation is indeterminate.

The right-of-first-offer condition — "no transfer of ownership shall take effect unless we or one of our affiliated companies first have the right to also offer consideration" — sets no time limit, no procedure and no consequence if the Company does not respond. Whether it merely requires an opportunity to bid or blocks transfer until the Company acts is unclear.

This restriction on transfers, including "a collateral or absolute assignment", is difficult to reconcile with Section 18, which permits you to "assign any interest in this policy without the consent of any person other than an irrevocable Beneficiary". The two sections set different conditions on the same act.

The paragraph is broken mid-sentence, so the condition preceding "your estate will be the Beneficiary" (evidently the absence of a surviving named beneficiary) is missing. As printed the default-beneficiary rule has no stated trigger.

The freedom to assign "without the consent of any person other than an irrevocable Beneficiary" runs against Section 17, which bars any transfer of ownership or collateral or absolute assignment for consideration until the Company has had the right to make a competing offer. The opening words "[e]xcept as otherwise provided in this policy" do not say which prevails.

The adjustment is to the benefit "that would have been purchased at the correct age or sex by the most recent Cost of Insurance charge deducted", a formula that uses one month's charge to reprice the whole face amount and reads as though words are missing. What the corrected benefit is cannot be computed from the sentence.

The operative promise is missing: the text opens "the Issue Date, except for any p ... insurability", so the words stating that the Company will not contest the policy after two years, and the exception, are absent. The core of the incontestability clause cannot be read from the provision.

The recovery is capped at "the higher of a return of any paid premium required by us for the contested face amount or the sum of any Monthly Deductions made under this policy for the contested face amount", but neither figure is defined for a flexible-premium policy where premiums are not allocated to particular face amounts. How to attribute premium or deductions to a "contested face amount" is unstated.

The integration clause is immediately qualified by the statement that later written requests "may become part of the policy", without saying when or how they do so. "May become part" leaves the boundary of the entire contract open.

That open-ended incorporation of later requests is hard to square with the following paragraph of the same section, which requires any change in the provisions of the policy to be in writing signed by an executive officer and countersigned. The section describes two inconsistent routes to amendment.

The reserved "right to correct any clerical errors in this policy, or in our administration of the policy" gives no definition of "clerical error" and no limit on retroactive correction. It could be read to reach substantive figures such as the Schedule's rates and charges.

The opening line is broken ("nniversary-we:will:send-you=-without-charge ach-Policy Year which-ineludes"), so when the statement is due and what it covers cannot be read from the text. The obligation survives only in the enumerated list.

This says the Company "may charge a reasonable fee, not to exceed $50" for an illustrative report requested at any other time, while the next paragraph promises "one report annually without charge". Whether the first annual request is free is not resolved.

The promise of "one report annually without charge" sits against the preceding paragraph, which allows a fee for any illustrative report requested "at any other time". The two fee rules overlap without a priority.

The rider's specification block appears as bare values ("SAME AS POLICY DATE $300.00 75% $250,000 $10,000") with the labels separated from them, so which figure is the Maximum Administrative Charge, the Maximum Proportion Allowable, the Maximum Accelerated Benefit or the Minimum Remaining Face Amount rests on inference. Other rider provisions expressly refer back to these "as specified in this rider".

Defining "We (Our, Us)" as "Phoenix Life Insurance Company, or its subsidiaries" conflicts with Section 3 of the policy, where "the terms 'we', 'us', and 'our' refer only to the Company". The rider states it is otherwise subject to all policy provisions.

The Eligible Amount excludes "any supplemental rider death benefits", a phrase that does not match any defined term in the policy, which speaks of a Supplemental Face Amount and of insurance provided by additional benefit riders. What is carved out of the death benefit is therefore uncertain.

Limitation 3 forbids a Proportion that produces a Requested Benefit "less than the lower of 25% of the policy face amount or $50,000", using a floor expressed through the lower of two figures, while limitation 2 refers to a minimum "as specified in this rider" whose label is detached from its value. The permissible range of election is hard to fix.

"Terminal Illness" turns on an illness "expected to result in the insured's death within six months based on evidence satisfactory to us", combining a prognosis standard with the insurer's own satisfaction. Who decides, and on what basis, is left to the insurer.

"Our discounting rate will be subject to the higher of: 1. 5%; or 2. the Published Monthly Average" does not say whether that higher figure is a ceiling or a floor on the rate used to discount the benefit. The direction of the constraint determines whether the insured is paid more or less.

The sentence is broken ("The discounted del any other 5 then current Administrative Charge"), so what is deducted from the discounted benefit besides the Administrative Charge cannot be read. The deduction that fixes the payment is incompletely stated.

The enumerated list is garbled (items run together with the stray characters "Oo PWN"), and it directs that "any policy debt including any unpaid loan interest" be "reduced by the Proportion" alongside the face amount and cash value. Whether the debt reduction is a benefit to the owner or a drafting slip is not resolvable from the text.

The paragraph presupposes a variable policy with Separate Account subaccounts, whereas this contract is a fixed-interest universal life policy whose Section 9 credits a declared interest rate. The provision has no subject matter in this instrument.

The statement that "[t]he policyowner will be responsible to pay the premiums ... in order to keep the policy in force" does not fit a flexible-premium policy, where Section 10 permits but never requires premium payments and Section 11 makes lapse turn on Policy Value. The rider imports a fixed-premium obligation the policy does not create.

The bar covers claims of "any creditor, trustee in bankruptcy or governmental agency, or arising under any court order directed against you", a general phrase appended to a specific list whose reach — for instance to a family-court or tax order — is unsettled. The qualifier "to the extent that we have written notice thereof" adds a further indeterminate limit.

The declaration is a compound negative — "no insured has applied to any insurance company or society without receiving the exact policy applied for or had any symptoms, diseases or disorders for which advice has been sought" — in which the "without" governs the first limb but not obviously the second. What exactly is being represented is uncertain, and rescission may turn on it.

The statement that "Home Office approval of form #519B is necessary before the policy is in effect" adds a condition of effectiveness not found in Section 10 of the policy or in the application's own list of conditions for insurance to take effect. The conditions precedent are stated in three places in different terms.

"Premiums are payable as shown on the schedule page of this policy" reads as a fixed obligation, whereas the policy is a flexible-premium contract in which the Schedule's Planned Premium is only an intention and Section 10 imposes no duty to pay. The two characterisations of the premium obligation differ.

The first-year figure of $299,526 does not match the application's Section V entries for first-year anticipated and subsequent planned premium. The amendment and the incorporated application state different premium figures.

The beneficiary section is reproduced with the sentences interleaved and the handwritten entries partly illegible, so the identity of the designated primary beneficiary and the share percentages cannot be read from the form itself. The default sharing rule is broken across the fragments.

The Total Face Amount applied for is illegible on the face of the form ("$_2)_ Jo, WD"), so the amount of coverage requested cannot be determined from this section. It is the operative figure of the coverage request.

The face amount recorded here does not correspond to the $6,000,000 stated in the Policy Acceptance Form amendment and the Schedule Pages. The application, which is made part of the policy, and the Schedule state the coverage differently.

The premium figures entered here ("103,397" and "453597") and the checked "Option 4 Level Face Amount" do not match the Schedule Pages' Planned Premium of $299,526 and "Death Benefit Option A". Since Section 22 makes the application part of the entire contract, the two documents state the terms differently.

The election refers to allocating premiums "to the Money Market subaccount until the end of the Right to Cancel Period, as stated in the policy", but this policy has no subaccounts and its front page provides a Right to Return with a full premium refund. The option described does not exist under the instrument.

The five conditions for the insurance to take effect — including that all representations "remain true, complete and accurate" and that there be no change in health — differ from Section 10 of the policy, which conditions coverage only on underwriting approval, satisfaction of the application conditions and receipt of the Minimum Initial Premium. They also sit against the Incontestability provision.
